transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Alyssa Chen (ScoutCap Head ML), Ben Rosario (VP Eng), Marco Silva (SRE), Priya Nair (Product)

Summary / Topics (auto): Per-token pricing discussion, batching and caching levers, deployment modes, security requirements (SOC2/KMS/SSO), pilot next steps.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intros?
[00:08] Alyssa: yep, alyssa here, i run ml at scoutcap. we do large scale extraction and narrative generation across financial filings, like pretty token heavy.
[00:16] Ben: ben, vp engineering. i'm here for capacity and budget side.
[00:20] Marco: marco, s-r-e. i'll be looking at networking and private deploy constraints.
[00:24] Maya: great. ethan and i will walk through economics and hosting options then dig into specific levers — batching, k-v cache, routing.
[00:30] Ethan: quick callout, if you have a current usage profile that helps— tokens per call, typical seq length, p95 latency targets.
[00:36] Alyssa: right now avg seq is 600 tokens, sometimes 1.2k for longer docs. about 120k requests / day, variable throughout trading hours. p95 target ~450ms for interactive product, but analytics jobs can be relaxed.
[00:50] Ben: and budget is tight, we're trying to keep monthly inference spend below $40k initially.
[00:56] Maya: ok that budget target is helpful. we usually map that to per-token thresholds and then recommend hosting modes.
[01:04] Ethan: rough sketch: hosted API is simplest — you pay per-token, we optimize batching and caching where possible; dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools which lowers per-token marginal cost at the expense of commit; private/VPC if you need your keys in KMS or strict residency and connectivity.
[01:22] Alyssa: can you quantify per-token difference? like 1) hosted baseline and 2) dedicated amortized?
[01:30] Maya: yes, we'll send exact sheet but ballpark — hosted for our mid-size models at your load might be $0.0025–0.003 per input token after batching; dedicated can drop effective per-token to something like $0.0015–0.002 depending on utilization and batch sizing.
[01:45] Marco: what's the main lever to move that number? caching? batching? quantization?
[01:50] Ethan: all of the above. batching increases GPU throughput but adds queuing latency; caching (prefix/KV) reduces repeated compute for similar prompts — big win for template-based flows; quantization reduces memory and allows denser packing on GPUs, sometimes smaller models with optimized kernels help.
[02:08] Ben: for our 120k req/day with avg 600 tokens, rough tokens/day is 72M. Multiply by per-token, that equals (Ben does rough math) — hosted is around $180–216k/month? that's way over budget.
[02:26] Alyssa: yeah that's why we wanted to talk; we need techniques to make that workable with $40k.
[02:32] Maya: right — a few strategies: 1) batch size tuning and dynamic batching windows during peaks; 2) heavy use of prefix/KV caching for repeated boilerplate; 3) route non-latency-sensitive jobs to cheaper model variants or scheduled batch jobs; 4) mix hosting: hosted for spikes + dedicated for baseline throughput; 5) token-slicing — truncate or summarize pre-pass to reduce tokens.
[02:57] Marco: can you explain the caching — prefix vs kv? i sometimes see K-V cache called 'K-V cash' in notes.
[03:04] Ethan: haha yes. prefix caching stores common prefix compute so you don't recompute for identical starts; KV cache is per-token key/value cache for autoregressive decoders reused across incremental tokens. in practice we shard and reuse across similar calls, that can reduce compute by 30–60% depending on repetition.
[03:22] Alyssa: our pipeline has a lot of repeated preamble and regulatory boilerplate — sounds promising.
[03:27] Ben: about batching, what's added latency at p95 if you go aggressive?
[03:33] Ethan: depends on batching window; at 5–10ms window you can coalesce a few requests with minimal latency. at 50–100ms you see more throughput but p95 increases. at your p95 target 450ms, we can tune to keep queuing under 50–80ms typically.
[03:48] Priya: and fallback policies — what if dedicated is saturated?
[03:52] Maya: we have smart routing and automated fallback to hosted or smaller variants. Redwood supports policies by latency or cost: if dedicated is busy, routing can failover to hosted or lower-cost region instance.
[03:59] Marco: any audit / security notes? we need SOC2, SSO, KMS. private on-prem might be required for some customers.
[04:05] Ethan: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and private control plane. we also provide SOC2 docs and audit logs; we can share our package. there's some lift for on-prem but doable.
[04:17] Ben: how different is unit economics for private on-prem vs dedicated in our cloud?
[04:22] Maya: private on-prem is more of a fixed cost with infra and ops overhead; per-token after amortization could be lower if you have very high utilization but you pick up ops costs. Dedicated in our cloud tends to be a middle ground — predictable SLA and we manage runtime ops.
[04:36] Alyssa: can we do a hybrid? e.g., private for the most sensitive workloads, dedicated for baseline analytics, hosted for spikes?
[04:42] Ethan: absolutely, that's a common pattern. routing policies let you tag requests by sensitivity and route accordingly.
[04:48] Ben: how about model variants — smaller models for batch jobs?
[04:51] Ethan: yes. using distilled or quantized variants for background jobs is common. Redwood Optimize can recommend quant profiles per workload but we can also run a small eval.
[05:00] Alyssa: i'm worried about the math — the 72M tokens/day example blew up to $200k. what's a pragmatic reduction path?
[05:08] Maya: step one, measure current repetition ratio (how often prefixes repeat); step two, pre-pass summarization — many long docs can be reduced; step three, route anomalies to smaller models; step four, consider commit to Dedicated for baseline to lower marginal. we can run a pilot to show numbers.
[05:22] Marco: network egress — if we host in our VPC what's the egress behavior?
[05:26] Ethan: for private/VPC deployments your traffic stays in VPC, no public egress. For hosted, obviously traffic goes to Redwood endpoints; we can set up private link in supported clouds to reduce egress.
[05:36] Priya: timeline — if we wanted to pilot in 4 weeks, is that realistic?
[05:40] Maya: yes, a 2–4 week pilot is typical: set up trial account, sample prompts, run benchmarks at different batch settings and cache configs, analyze unit cost.
[05:47] Ben: what about burst capacity? during earnings we spike 5x. how to cover that without overcommitting?
[05:52] Ethan: dedicate baseline capacity for predictable load and enable burst to hosted or on-demand instances; we can also schedule pre-warm windows. bursts are billed differently but you avoid hard outages.
[06:02] Alyssa: can we see an example calc — how batching improves cost?
[06:06] Maya: absolutely. e.g., naive per-token compute cost 0.000... (Maya explains numbers) — when you go from micro-batches of 1 to effective batch of 8–16 the GPU utilization jumps and effective per-token drops by roughly 30% depending on model and seq length.
[06:24] Speaker 1: (inaudible) question about p50 vs p95 skew.
[06:28] Ethan: if your p95 is the constraining SLO we bias scheduling for it. background batches can be queued more aggressively.
[06:34] Ben: any gotchas with quantization? sometimes quality drops and we risk hallucinations.
[06:39] Ethan: yeah quality tradeoffs — we usually run eval sets; Redwood Optimize suggests quantization knobs per-prompt and we tie regression alerts to eval sets. you'll want to run prior to wide rollout.
[06:51] Alyssa: what about caching warmup — is it per-container? if we use dedicated, do we lose cache on scale down?
[06:57] Ethan: good q — KV cache is tied to inference containers' state and is ephemeral; we have shared cache layers for prefix reuse across containers but cold starts reduce hit rate. autoscaling can be tuned to prefer steady capacity to avoid churn.
[07:12] Marco: our SREs want to know what observability we get.
[07:16] Maya: console provides token-level cost, latency breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and hooks for traces; we can push logs to your ingestion.
[07:24] Marco: audit logs?
[07:26] Ethan: yes, we surface audit logs, API key usage, and per-request metadata useful for compliance.
[07:31] Priya: any reference customers in finance?
[07:34] Maya: we've worked with a few fintechs and reg-data workloads. i can share anonymized case studies and a couple of reference contacts under NDA.
[07:42] Alyssa: ok, let's talk concrete pilot scope. we want: 1) measure current baseline cost at current prompt set; 2) test caching effectiveness for boilerplate; 3) tune batching windows to keep p95 < 450ms; 4) evaluate a dedicated baseline vs hosted marginal.
[07:58] Maya: sounds good — we'll scope a 2–3 week pilot that runs representative traffic, we instrument cost and quality.
[08:05] Ben: for billing during pilot — is it just hosted per-token or do you have trial credits?
[08:10] Maya: we typically provide trial credits and discount guidance for pilots; we can also provide a pilot price model so you can see projected monthly costs.
[08:18] Alyssa: please also include steps for private/VPC if needed.
[08:21] Ethan: will do. for VPC we need your network ranges and firewall rules; Marco can share a short checklist and we can map timeline.
[08:30] Marco: will share network constraints offline.
[08:33] Maya: ok i'll summarize next steps. ethan will provision the sandbox, i'll send pricing worksheet, alyssa/ben send prompt set and SLOs, marco send network checklist.
[08:42] Priya: any blockers on our side? we might need legal to sign an NDA for references.
[08:47] Maya: that's fine, we can route through legal.
[08:50] Speaker 2: (brief laughter)
[08:52] Ethan: one last note — we can run small A/B comparing quantized variant quality vs full precision on your prompts to check degradation.
[08:59] Alyssa: yes please.
[09:02] Maya: all right, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the workbook and sandbox invite.
[09:07] Ben: thanks.
[09:09] Marco: thanks.

(roughly 48 minutes elapsed; end of recording)
